extracted.intended_audience: classical philologists, textual editors, translators, and advanced students of Aristotle and ancient Greek literature
extracted.subtask_description: Scholarly guidelines and critical principles for establishing, emending, and interpreting the text of Aristotle's Poetics and for understanding its poetic-theoretical claims (genre, parts, and methods).

rubrics_metrics.name: General tests for accepting emendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Before accepting any alteration it should be submitted to the ruthless criticism taught in the Topics: Does it violate Greek usage? Does it disagree with the author's system? Does it make the author say or suggest anything which he wished to avoid?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these three questions as primary filters for proposed emendations. Examples: avoid accepting changes that produce solecistic syntax or that contradict Aristotle's doctrines elsewhere (see examples 1451 b 30, 1450 a 17).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rearrangement or displacement of the text
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the whole text is arranged with the care and ingenuity of a puzzle, any sort of rearrangement or displacement is likely to spread havoc far and wide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reorder sentences or phrases unless there is compelling internal and external evidence; modern or Renaissance rearrangements often do more harm than good. Example: rearrangements attributed to Lascaris and other editors frequently corrupt argument and syntax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect original sentence construction and syntax
rubrics_metrics.description: Preserve the sentence construction; alterations that ruin syntax or make the argument unintelligible are unacceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete example: removing καὶ δυνατὰ γενέσθαι from 1451 b 30 renders the syntax solecistic and destroys the argument. Verify that proposed deletions or insertions preserve Greek grammatical relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not accept readings solely because foreign versions 'confirm' them
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere fact that the Arabic or Syriac ‘confirms’ a reading does not prove its genuineness; these versions may reflect interpolated or corrupted texts or translator idiosyncrasies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat Arabic/Syriac evidence cautiously; check whether their underlying Greek was already interpolated or interpreted. Examples: Arabic anticipating nineteenth-century emendations; Arabic following an interpolated text (Bernays case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess scribe competence and habits when weighing manuscript readings
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the behavior, competence, and known practices of particular scribes or manuscript groups (e.g., bold emendation vs. leaving blanks, contamination from other copies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: AposTo.is copied many MSS and likely did not emend boldly; some scribes leave blanks in difficult passages whereas Lascaris made bold corrections. Use knowledge of scribe habits to judge likelihood of originality vs. later correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be alert to doctrinal or cultural influence on readings
rubrics_metrics.description: Readings may have been altered for ideological or doctrinal reasons (e.g., Christian euphemism or avoidance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: παθημάτων changed to μαθημάτων (Definition of Tragedy) possibly to avoid Christian objections; διαμένειν altered to a less offensive construction. When a reading seems to neutralize offence, consider motive and weigh against internal evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for common scribal omissions (homoeoteleuton)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gradual loss of matter in MSS often results from inaccurate copying, with homoeoteleuton a frequent cause of omission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare witnesses to recover omitted words; some codices (e.g., A) suffer less, others more. Seek corroboration in other manuscripts or versions before emending for omission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer readings consistent with the author's system and other works
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Aristotle’s doctrines and parallel passages (Politics, Nicomachean Ethics, Meteorology, Topics, etc.) to judge contested readings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: determining the proper form for statements about courage in women by reference to Aristotle’s Politics and Ethics. Readings that contradict Aristotle’s systematic positions are suspect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret translator idiosyncrasy and paraphrase cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: Translators (Syriac, Arabic) sometimes paraphrase, misinterpret, or introduce conjectural glosses; they may treat one vernacular as primary and re-interpret.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a version is literal, paraphrastic, or shaped by the translator’s own confusion (e.g., Asu’l-BasHar treating Syriac as original or producing fanciful renderings). Do not take paraphrase as confirmation of Greek original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emend only when Greek usage and grammar support the change
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed emendations must satisfy Greek idiom and syntactical norms; avoid readings that produce un-Greek structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: ἰατρικὸν ἢ φυσικόν is bad Greek because the connective should separate distinct genera; prefer readings that restore proper coordination (e.g., φυσικὸν καὶ ἰατρικόν).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be suspicious of easy additions or plausible amplifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists, convenient clarifications, or neat additions are easy to insert and therefore suspect as later interpolations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the ‘five substantives’ list could be readily added; similarly adding sigma to masculine terminations is an obvious interpolation. Treat solitary or unique additions with caution unless supported by good witnesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for orthographic corruptions (itacism, dittography) in variant readings
rubrics_metrics.description: Some corruptions result from phonetic errors (itacism) or accidental letter repetitions (dittography).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: εἴδει corrupted by itacism or dittography to ἢ δεινὴν εἶναι; identify plausible orthographic processes before positing semantic emendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer witnesses showing signs of greater antiquity, but weigh contamination
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers or codices exhibiting more signs of antiquity (e.g., E) should be given weight, yet contamination and shared errors require careful genealogical analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: E often quoted in apparatus because it shows antiquity; but agreement between MSS may derive from common contamination rather than direct descent—do not assume simple stemma without testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use cross-references to related treatises to resolve obscure terms or metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: Opaque words or metaphors in Poetics can often be clarified by consulting Aristotle’s other works (e.g., Meteorology clarifies references to φλόξ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: interpret φλόξ as meteoric flame by reference to Meteorology; explicating proportion metaphors requires cross-textual reading to restore intended sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: When reconstructing technical lists or taxonomies, honor the author’s conceptual distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques of classification (genus/differentia, function/species) should be restored consistent with the author’s analytic scheme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the treatment that 'function corresponds with the species' (Politics) should inform how lists or taxonomic phrases are emended; don't force modern taxonomies onto Aristotle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal (poiesis) criteria: poetry as 'immaterial portrayal of the imaginary'
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitional criterion: poetry (poiesis) is fabrication/portrayal of the imaginary (not the actual); it differs from history by portraying the general and the possible rather than the particular actuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this definition to evaluate poetic works: judge whether a work constructs typical/idealized actions (possible under moral certainty) rather than merely reporting events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three bases of poetic classification (Clothing, Theme, Treatment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic varieties differ in (1) Clothing (medium/category: rhythm, language, harmony), (2) Theme (species of subject matter: good, bad, average), and (3) Treatment (mode: narration vs impersonation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying or composing a work, specify which of these three axes is operative. They are ordered by importance and cross-cut each other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy’s evaluative criterion: portrays actions/career, not mere qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is mimesis not of men but of action and life (faring); the genus is a career (πρᾶξις), the end is a career, not a quality—tragic plot should represent actions with unity and causal structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In creating or judging tragedies prefer plots that show causally integrated actions (the ‘career’) rather than scenes designed only to display character traits. Use Topics/Metaphysics analogies (genus/differentia) to test adequacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Components of poetic form to be evaluated/used: rhythm, language, harmony
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry/clothing is realized through Rhythm (dance/metre), Language (prose/verse), and Harmony (tunes, not chords), which may be separate or mixed and determine the medium’s effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For composition or criticism, identify which components are present and how they function (e.g., language + rhythm = verse; harmony + dance = musical performance). Assess whether the chosen combination suits the theme and treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative vs reproductive portrayal and ideal vs realistic depiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Creative (poetic) portrayal generalizes and fabricates (gathers ideal traits), while reproductive art copies particulars; artistic likeness (ideal) synthesizes best features, realistic likeness portrays as-is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a work, judge whether it aims at typification (artistic/ideal) or faithful reproduction (realistic/photographic), and whether that aim is successfully achieved. Use this to explain audience response and artistic value.
